opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think about it a lot. The framing I keep coming back to is: what would actually change what happens with frontier models? It's very easy in research to work on something that's intellectually satisfying, produces a nice paper, and then just doesn't matter, because nobody building or deploying these systems would ever use it.

So the first filter I apply is a kind of theory of impact. If this project goes really well, who does something differently? Maybe a lab uses it to catch a model being deceptive in an evaluation. Maybe it gives us a better way to audit a model before deployment. Maybe it just shifts the field's understanding of how these systems work, so other people build better tools. If I can't tell a fairly concrete story there, that's a warning sign.

The second thing is being honest about what actually works. I've updated a lot here over the years. Coming from mechanistic interpretability, there's a temptation to want the beautiful, complete understanding of a model, and I still think that's a worthwhile long-term goal. But I've become much more pragmatic. If a simple baseline like a linear probe, or just reading the model's chain of thought, gets you most of the way on a safety-relevant task, you should know that, and you should compare your fancy method against it. A lot of my thinking now is about whether interpretability tools beat the boring alternatives on problems people actually care about.

Third, I try to work on things that will still matter as models get more capable. Some techniques work fine on today's models but you can tell they'd break the moment the model is smart enough to route around them. I'd rather invest in approaches that degrade gracefully, or that we can stress-test with model organisms, where you deliberately train a model to have some bad property and see whether your method catches it.

And finally there's comparative advantage, both for me personally and for the people I mentor. Being close to frontier models gives you access and context that's really valuable, so I lean toward problems where that matters. Whereas some foundational work can be done perfectly well by academics or independent researchers with open-weight models, and it's great when they do.

So the short version is: pick problems with a clear path to changing real decisions, be ruthlessly empirical about whether your method actually helps, and favor things that will scale to the models we're worried about, not just the ones we have.

r001.rationale: It presents several distinct ways safety research could improve outcomes, including deception detection, predeployment audits, better interpretability tools, and approaches that scale to more capable models.

r002.rationale: It says to favor techniques that remain useful as models become more capable and scale to the models of concern.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that I've changed my mind on this quite a lot over the past few years. When I got into interpretability I had this fairly grand vision, where the goal was to completely reverse-engineer a model, understand every circuit, and then you'd just be able to read off whether it was deceptive or misaligned. And I think that was a mistake, or at least a mistake as a near-term plan. The models are enormous, they're messy, and I don't think we're going to get a complete understanding of them before we have systems that really matter.

So the way I think about it now is much more pragmatic. The question I ask is: what is the actual threat model, what would a lab need to be able to do to catch it or prevent it, and is there a research direction where partial progress still buys you something? Interpretability is a good example. Even if you only understand ten percent of what's going on inside a model, that ten percent might be enough to build a probe that flags when the model is thinking about something it shouldn't be, or to give you evidence when you're trying to figure out whether some weird behaviour is a quirk or something more concerning. You don't need the full picture to get real safety value.

The second heuristic is that I try to work backwards from how a result would actually get used. There's a lot of safety research that's intellectually interesting but if you ask "okay, who at a frontier lab picks this up, and what decision does it change?", there's no good answer. So I like projects where I can picture the deployment story. Like, this becomes part of a monitoring stack, or this becomes a tool an alignment team uses when they're red-teaming a model before release, or this gives you a signal that complements evals and black-box methods rather than competing with them.

And I'd flag that I think the field underrates how much you can learn from the models we already have. People sometimes say "well, current models aren't dangerous, so studying them doesn't tell you about the dangerous ones." But the techniques, the tooling, the intuitions you build, those all transfer. And honestly, it's very hard to do good empirical research on a hypothetical. So I'd rather do rigorous work on real systems, be very honest about where it does and doesn't generalise, and iterate as the models change.

The last thing I'd say, especially for people thinking about getting into this, is that research taste matters a lot here, and the main way you build it is by doing things and being wrong. I've spent plenty of time on directions that didn't pan out. That's fine. The failure mode I'd actually worry about is picking something because it sounds important and then never checking whether the work is cashing out into anything that makes the models safer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses multiple possible research directions, including interpretability, monitoring, red-teaming, and empirical work, and frames choosing among them as a pragmatic safety problem.

r002.rationale: The response says techniques developed on current models can transfer, urges honesty about what generalizes, and recommends iterating as models change.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with: what’s the actual safety problem you’re trying to solve, and why do you think your research would help? It’s quite easy to pick something technically interesting, make progress on it, and have a vague story that this will eventually be useful for safety. I think you want a more concrete connection than that.

For mechanistic interpretability, for example, understanding what’s happening inside a model is a research ambition. But a safety application might be: can we detect a dangerous behaviour that our behavioural evaluations missed? Can we understand why a safeguard fails, and use that understanding to improve it? Those give you something to test against.

And I’d want to compare against simpler approaches. If looking at the model’s activations gives you a signal, does it actually tell you something you couldn’t get by asking the model questions or examining its outputs? Sometimes the answer will be no, and that’s useful to learn early.

There’s still room for exploratory research. You often don’t know what a technique will be good for until you’ve developed it a bit. But I’d keep coming back to the question: if this succeeds, what decision could someone building or evaluating a frontier model make differently? That helps distinguish an interesting result from one that could actually make a model safer.

r001.rationale: It discusses multiple ways safety research might help, but does not characterize frontier model safety as a problem with many possible directions for improvement.

r002.rationale: It asks what decision a frontier model builder or evaluator could make differently if the research succeeds, tying the research to the models it aims to make safer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point should be: what’s a concrete way these models could cause harm, and what would need to change to make that less likely? It’s very easy to pick an interesting technical problem, make progress on it, and then tell a story about why that progress is useful for safety. I want the safety problem to do more of the work in choosing the research.

For interpretability, for example, understanding some feature inside a model isn’t automatically a safety contribution. I want to know what decision that understanding could change. Could we detect a dangerous capability that behavioural evaluations missed? Could we identify why a safeguard fails, and use that to build a better one? What evidence would convince us that our method actually works?

And I’d put a lot of weight on getting feedback from real models and realistic settings. Start with a threat model, build the smallest useful test, and be willing to discover that your approach doesn’t help. There’s a balance here: you need room for exploratory research, because we don’t know which ideas will pay off. But you also need to keep checking the connection between an intellectually satisfying result and something that could actually make a frontier model safer.

r001.rationale: It presents several potential safety research directions, including detecting dangerous capabilities and improving safeguards, and says exploratory research is needed because it is unclear which ideas will pay off.

r002.rationale: It calls for feedback from real models and realistic settings, testing whether an approach helps, and checking its connection to making frontier models safer.
